items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1969-12-04
items.q: And my brother played with the finest officers, with Johnny Green, played with Alfred Newman.

ctx.x: You want to get it going again? Okay.

Yeah, it's all right. I would rather it be known because I, truthfully, in spite of the fact that I thought he was more or less a mountainebank, now that's not a good thing to say, but he wasn't a musician he was talented to be, and he couldn't sing a lick, but he thought he could. But he was the finest gentleman you ever met. His whole heart was in music, and he liked me, and I turned on him. Only in this respect, that when he asked me for an interview, I said, what's the matter, you ran out of Negroes? Because…
Well, it may not have been his fault, you know. It may have been some pressure put on him by the publishers or something of the book.

items.title: Johnny DeDroit Interview, 1973-03-16
items.q: He wasn't my very best. Gershwin?

ctx.x: He wasn't my very best. Gershwin? Gershwin, yeah. I used to love to play that. You know, I've been out since 59, and there's this think tank going back on me, you know. Not too badly. You have to live in that life to keep up with it, you know. I knew a million tunes. We could play. We had so many composers in the band, and some nights the cars would play only our own tunes. Yeah, well I wrote a lot of tunes. Yeah, well I wrote a lot of tunes. They always wanted to, I wasn't smart. If I could give them Jack Mills…

You know what I mean? Do you think that the people here in New Orleans request a lot of the music that was particularly, say, associated with this area and by composers like, say, Jilly Roll Morton or other people that were local?
